adults.title: More Than Missing a Meal
adults.big_idea: When we fast as an act of worship, joined with earnest prayer and generous giving, we draw nearer to the Savior and He answers, “Here I am.”
adults.objective: Learners will be able to explain what makes a fast an act of worship and will write a simple plan for their next fast: a purpose, a prayer, and an offering.
prepare: Read Elder Soares’s talk and Isaiah 58:3–11 before class.
Write on the board: Fast Sunday is ______.
Bring a small card or slip of paper and a pen for each person.
Mark the three key quotes below so you can find them quickly.
Be aware that some class members cannot go without food for health reasons. Keep the focus on worship, prayer, and generosity, which everyone can offer.

segments.name: An honest start
steps: Begin with prayer. Point to the board and invite everyone to finish the sentence silently and honestly: Fast Sunday is ______.
Invite them to turn to a neighbor and share their word, and why. Take two or three answers from the class. Welcome honest ones such as long, hard, or easy to forget.

Explain that Elder Ulisses Soares of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles invited us to live the law of the fast in a higher and holier way. Today we will look for what that means and choose one thing to do about it.
questions: What is the difference between going without food and fasting?

segments.name: What Isaiah saw
steps: Explain that Elder Soares taught that in Isaiah 58 the Lord lifted His people’s vision beyond the outward observance of this law.
Divide the class into two groups. Group one reads Isaiah 58:3–7 and looks for what the Lord says a fast is for. Group two reads Isaiah 58:8–11 and lists every promise the Lord makes.
After four minutes, invite each group to report. Write their findings in two columns on the board: The fast the Lord chooses, and What He promises.
Read the first key quote aloud (the tender promise). Let it rest for a moment before asking the question.
questions: Which of these promises do you most need right now, and why?

segments.name: Fasting and prayer: the Savior’s pattern
steps: Invite someone to read Matthew 4:1–2. Explain that Elder Soares taught that, of all the things the Savior could have done to prepare for His mission, He chose to seek complete alignment with His Father’s will through earnest fasting and prayer.
Read the second key quote (fasting and prayer may not remove every burden). Then read the words of Elder Chigbundu from this conference, listed under aligned quotes.
Ask the first question and give a full minute of silence before anyone answers. Invite two or three people to share. Thank each one; do not add to their experience.
Read Helaman 3:35 together and add to the board what happened to those who fasted and prayed often.
questions: When has fasting and prayer not changed your circumstance but changed you?
Elder Soares said fasting is more than a petition for specific blessings. What changes when we fast to understand the Lord’s will rather than only to ask for something?

segments.name: Looking beyond ourselves
steps: Explain that Elder Soares taught that our desire to help the oppressed go free finds tangible expression in generous fast offerings.
Read the words of the Prophet Joseph Smith that Elder Soares quoted, listed under aligned quotes.

Read Alma 7:11–12 together. Ask learners to look for why the Savior took upon Himself our pains and afflictions. Explain that Elder Soares taught that as we follow His example by seeking to succor God’s children, our hearts are opened to the needs of others.
Read the third key quote (small and simple offerings) and ask the question.
questions: How does giving a fast offering change the way you feel during a fast, or the way you see the people around you?

segments.name: Plan my next fast
steps: Give each person a card. Ask them to write three words down the side: Purpose, Prayer, Offering.

Give two minutes of silent writing. Beside each word they write one line: what they will fast for or about, when they will kneel to begin and end their fast, and how they will give generously of their means or time.
As a check for understanding, invite each person to tell a neighbor in one sentence what makes a fast higher and holier. Listen for worship, prayer, and care for others.

segments.name: Invitation and promise
steps: Read Elder Soares’s invitation and the promise that follows it, both listed below. Read slowly.
Share in a sentence or two your own witness that the Lord draws near when we call on Him. Invite learners to keep their card in their scriptures until the next fast Sunday.
Follow up: next week, or after the next fast Sunday, begin class by asking who would share what was different about their fast.

key_quotes.text: What a tender promise: light after darkness, healing after weariness, and the comforting assurance that when we call upon the Lord, He is near.

His example teaches us that fasting and prayer may not remove every burden from our path, but they draw heaven near and endow us with divine power to overcome or endure whatever circumstances we may face, giving us the spiritual fortitude to remain faithful to the Father’s will.
Though our fast offerings may seem small and simple, they become consecrated expressions of compassion, concern, and service.

As you do so, I promise, in the name of our Savior, Jesus Christ, that miracles will come into your life. You will draw nearer to the Savior, receive strength to overcome your weaknesses, and become more sensitive to the needs of others.

scriptures.use: Two groups: one reads verses 3–7 to find what the Lord says a fast is for; the other reads verses 8–11 and lists every promise. Record both lists on the board.
Read aloud before discussing how the Savior prepared for His ministry through fasting and prayer.
Read together; list what happened to those who fasted and prayed often.
Read together; look for why the Savior took upon Himself our pains and afflictions, then connect it to caring for those in need through fast offerings.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Chigbundu
aligned_quotes.text: The burden we carry may not always be removed, but our backs will be built to carry the load placed upon them

aligned_quotes.speaker: The Prophet Joseph Smith
aligned_quotes.text: A man filled with the love of God, is not content with blessing his family alone, but ranges through the whole world, anxious to bless the whole human race.

invitations.text: I invite you to prayerfully ponder Isaiah’s teachings and more intentionally embrace the divine purpose of the law of the fast in a higher and holier way as part of our worship.

takeaways: A fast is worship, not only going without food.
Fasting joined with prayer draws heaven near, even when the burden stays.
A generous fast offering turns my fast toward God’s children.
act: Before the next fast Sunday, read Isaiah 58:6–11 prayerfully and choose one promise to seek.
Begin and end your next fast on your knees, telling the Lord the purpose of your fast and asking to understand His will.
Decide ahead of time what a generous fast offering looks like for you, and give it with a prayer for those it will bless.
During your fast, ask the Lord who needs you, and act on the name that comes.
music: Because I Have Been Given Much
adapt: At home: read Isaiah 58:6–9 together, then make one family card with a shared purpose, a time to pray together, and an offering.
Large class: have pairs, not groups, read the Isaiah verses, and take reports from only three or four pairs.
Short on time: keep the Isaiah reading, the second key quote, and the planning card. Leave out Helaman 3:35.

youth.title: Hungry or Fasting?
youth.big_idea: Fasting is more than skipping meals: with real prayer and generosity it brings us closer to Jesus Christ and gives us strength we do not have on our own.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to explain the difference between going hungry and fasting, and will design their own plan for the next fast Sunday.
prepare: Read Elder Soares’s talk and Isaiah 58:6–11.
Bring a slip of paper and a pen for each person, plus a few extra sheets for teams.
Write on the board: Going hungry / Fasting, as two column headings.
Ask the youth to bring scriptures or to have Gospel Library open on their phones.
Be gentle: some youth cannot safely go without food. Keep the focus on worship, prayer, and giving, and leave how each person fasts to them, their parents, and the Lord.

segments.name: One honest word
steps: As soon as class begins, hand out slips of paper. Ask everyone to write one honest word for how fast Sunday usually feels. No names.
Collect the slips and read several aloud without comment. Smile at the honest ones.
Point to the two columns on the board and ask the question. Take quick answers and write them under each heading.
Say that Elder Ulisses Soares of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles invited us to live this law in a higher and holier way. Today we find out what that looks like.
questions: If two people skip the same two meals, what makes one of them hungry and the other one fasting?

segments.name: Promise hunt
steps: Offer a short prayer if you have not yet. Then form teams of two or three and give each team a sheet of paper.
Set a timer for three minutes. Teams search Isaiah 58:8–11 and list every promise the Lord makes to those who fast His way. The longest accurate list wins.
Have the winning team read their list. Other teams add anything missed.
Ask each person to pick the one promise they most want right now and tell their team why.
questions: Which promise would make the biggest difference in your life this month?

segments.name: What makes it a fast
steps: Read Isaiah 58:6–7 aloud. Ask: according to these verses, who else is a fast supposed to help?
Read the first key quote (a sincere and faithful fast). Write on the board under Fasting: a purpose, real prayer, generous giving.
Read the words of President Joseph F. Smith that Elder Soares quoted, listed under aligned quotes. Ask the first question.

Explain fast offerings simply: we give what we can to help people in need. Elder Soares taught that even offerings that seem small and simple become expressions of compassion, and that we can consecrate both our means and our time.
questions: What does it mean for your spirit to be in charge of your body? Where else in your life would that help?
Praying while fasting can feel different from a normal prayer. Why do you think that is?

segments.name: What if nothing changes?
steps: In pairs, skim Matthew 4:1–11. Ask pairs to notice what the Savior did before His ministry began and what He was able to do afterward.
Read the second key quote (fasting and prayer may not remove every burden).

Say that it is fair to ask what happens when we fast for something and it does not turn out the way we hoped. Read the third key quote (even when answers do not come) and then Elder Dunn’s words, listed under aligned quotes.
Ask the question. Let them answer honestly. Do not rush to fix every answer.
questions: Elder Soares says fasting is more than a petition for specific blessings. If that is true, what is a fast for?

segments.name: Design your fast
steps: Hand out fresh slips of paper. Each person designs their next fast in three lines: my purpose (who or what I am fasting for), my prayers (when I will pray to start and to end), my giving (something generous I will do with my own money or time).
Give three minutes of quiet writing. Write your own plan while they write.
Invite them to share one line of their plan with a partner.
Check for understanding: ask each person to write, in one sentence a friend at school would understand, why members of the Church of Jesus Christ fast. Invite two or three to read theirs.

segments.name: Invitation and promise
steps: Read Elder Soares’s invitation, listed below. Then read the promise that follows it (the fourth key quote).
Invite them to take a photo of their plan or put it where they will see it on the next fast Sunday.
Follow up: on the Sunday after the next fast Sunday, start class by asking what was different this time.

key_quotes.text: A sincere and faithful fast is accompanied by earnest and intentional prayer.

His example teaches us that fasting and prayer may not remove every burden from our path, but they draw heaven near and endow us with divine power to overcome or endure whatever circumstances we may face

Even when answers do not come in the way we expect, fasting and prayer help us develop greater confidence in the Lord, in our covenants with Him, and in His plan for our lives, as well as a deeper willingness to accept His will.

As you do so, I promise, in the name of our Savior, Jesus Christ, that miracles will come into your life. You will draw nearer to the Savior, receive strength to overcome your weaknesses, and become more sensitive to the needs of others.

scriptures.use: Promise hunt: teams have three minutes to list every promise the Lord makes; then each person chooses the one they most want.
Read aloud; ask who else a fast is supposed to help.
Skim in pairs; notice what the Savior did before His ministry began and what He was able to do afterward.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Joseph F. Smith
aligned_quotes.text: would … place the body in subjection to the spirit, and so promote communion with the Holy Ghost

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Dunn
aligned_quotes.text: Peace will come even when hoped-for outcomes do not.

invitations.text: I invite you to prayerfully ponder Isaiah’s teachings and more intentionally embrace the divine purpose of the law of the fast in a higher and holier way as part of our worship.

takeaways: Fasting without prayer is just going hungry.
Fasting and prayer bring heaven close and give me strength, even when the problem stays.
My fast is also for someone else: I give to help people in need.
act: Follow your three-line plan on the next fast Sunday: a purpose, a prayer to start and to end, and something generous.
Read Isaiah 58:6–11 on your phone the night before and choose one promise to look for.
Give a fast offering from your own money, even if it is small, or give an hour of your time to someone who needs it.
Afterward, write down one thing you felt or noticed, and be ready to share it in class.
adapt: At home: do the promise hunt as parents against youth, then write one plan together for a family fast.
Small class: skip teams and do the promise hunt as one group racing the timer.
Short on time: keep the opening word, the promise hunt, and the three-line plan.

children.title: We Pray and We Share
children.big_idea: Fasting is a special way to come closer to Heavenly Father and Jesus: we pray, and we share with people who need help.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that when we fast we pray and we share, and will choose one way to pray or share this week.
prepare: Bring a flashlight, a blanket, a picture of the Savior, paper, and a box of crayons.
Place the picture of the Savior at the front of the room where every child can see it.
Be ready to sing “A Child’s Prayer.”
Do not ask children to go without food. Parents guide when and how their children begin to fast. Today the children practice praying and sharing.

segments.name: Sing and pray
steps: Invite a child to pray. Sing “A Child’s Prayer” together.
Ask the question and let several children answer.
Say: Today we will learn about a special way to feel close to Heavenly Father and Jesus. It is called fasting.
questions: How do you feel when you talk to Heavenly Father in prayer?

segments.name: Light like the morning
steps: Explain simply: When people fast, they choose to go without food for a little while. They do it to think about Heavenly Father, to pray, and to share with people who need help.
Turn off the lights if the room allows. Hold the flashlight under the blanket, switched on, so the light is hidden. Ask: Can you see much light?
Let a child pull the blanket away. Say: The prophet Isaiah said that when we fast the way the Lord asks, light comes like the morning, and when we call to the Lord He says, “Here I am.”
Teach the short truth with actions: We pray (fold arms) and we share (open hands). Say it together three times.

segments.name: Jesus fasted and prayed
steps: Lay the blanket on the floor to be a quiet place. Tell the story: Before Jesus began teaching the people, He went to a quiet place called the wilderness. He fasted and prayed for 40 days to be close to His Father.
Invite the children to walk on quiet feet to the blanket and kneel or sit with arms folded. Count to 40 together softly by tens, showing ten fingers each time.
Say: Fasting and praying made Jesus strong to choose the right. Invite the children to stand up tall and strong.
Ask the question.
questions: Why do you think Jesus wanted to be close to His Father?

segments.name: Steps closer to Jesus
steps: Have the children line up at the back of the room, facing the picture of the Savior.
Explain: I will say something a child might do. If it helps us come closer to Jesus, take one step forward. If it does not, stand still as a statue.
Call out, one at a time: saying a prayer, sharing a toy, grabbing something from a friend, helping someone who is sad, saying unkind words, giving to help people in need, thanking Heavenly Father.

When the children reach the picture, say: Elder Soares, an Apostle of Jesus Christ, promised that when we fast in a higher and holier way, we will draw nearer to the Savior. Repeat together: We pray and we share.

segments.name: Sharing the crayons
steps: Sit in a circle. Give the whole box of crayons to one helper and a blank paper to every child. Ask: Can everyone draw? What could we do?
Let the helper share the crayons until every child has some. Ask how it felt to give and how it felt to receive.
Explain: When people fast, they also give a fast offering. That is money they share so people who need food or other help can have what they need.

Tell the children in your own words what President Eyring shared at this conference, quoting President Spencer W. Kimball: Heavenly Father watches over us, and He often helps people through another person. We can be that person.
questions: Who is someone you could share with or help this week?

segments.name: Draw: I pray, I share
steps: Have each child fold their paper in half. On one side they draw themselves praying. On the other side they draw themselves sharing or helping someone.
Walk around and ask each child to tell you about their drawing. Write I pray and I share at the top for those who want help.
Check for understanding: ask each child, one at a time, What do we do when we fast? Listen for: we pray and we share.

segments.name: Choose and close
steps: Invite each child to point to one side of their drawing and choose it as the thing they will do this week.
Share your testimony in one or two sentences: Heavenly Father hears our prayers, and Jesus is happy when we share.
Ask the children to take their drawing home and show their family. Follow up: next week, ask who prayed or shared, and let them tell about it.

key_quotes.text: when we call upon the Lord, He is near
You will draw nearer to the Savior, receive strength to overcome your weaknesses, and become more sensitive to the needs of others.

scriptures.use: After the flashlight activity, read verse 9 aloud (or have an older child read it) and ask what the Lord says when we call to Him.
Tell this story in your own words while the children act it out; an older child can read verse 2 aloud.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Spencer W. Kimball, quoted by President Eyring
aligned_quotes.text: God does notice us, and he watches over us. But it is usually through another person that he meets our needs.

takeaways: Heavenly Father hears me when I pray.
Jesus fasted and prayed to be close to His Father.
I can share to help people in need.
act: Say a prayer this week and thank Heavenly Father for three things.
Share something of yours with a brother, sister, or friend.
Show your drawing to your family and tell them: we pray and we share.
On the next fast Sunday, ask a grown-up if you can help by saying a prayer for someone who needs help.

adapt.younger: Ages 3–7: Keep each part short and repeat We pray and we share with the actions after every activity. Use only four statements in the stepping game and say the answer with them. Let a helper hold the flashlight. For the drawing, one picture is enough: me praying.
adapt.older: Ages 8–11: Have a child read Isaiah 58:9 and another read Matthew 4:2. Let an older child lead the stepping game and think of statements. Ask: Fasting did not take away every hard thing for Jesus. How did it help Him? Invite them to write one sentence under each drawing.
